input.strategy_title: Audit logging for model inference traffic
input.strategy_markdown:
## Problem Statement

Financial-services customers cannot pass compliance reviews because inference
traffic on RHOAI leaves no audit trail: there is no record of who invoked which
model endpoint, when, and with what outcome. Auditors require tamper-evident,
structured audit events for every inference request. Without this, two
strategic renewals are at risk this fiscal year.

## High-Level Requirements

| ID | Priority | Requirement |
|-------|----------|-------------|
| HLR-1 | P0 | Every inference request through a KServe endpoint emits an audit event capturing caller identity, model/version, timestamp, and response status (not payloads). |
| HLR-2 | P0 | Audit events are delivered to the cluster audit sink with at-least-once semantics and are not lost on component restart. |
| HLR-3 | P1 | Administrators can enable/disable inference auditing per project from the Dashboard. |
| HLR-4 | P2 | A common audit event schema is defined and published so future components (pipelines, workbenches) emit compatible events. Note: the schema in this item is the format HLR-1's events must conform to — HLR-1 cannot ship before the schema is settled. |
| HLR-5 | P2 | Documentation covers enabling auditing and interpreting events. |

## Affected Components

- KServe
- Dashboard

## Out of Scope

- Auditing of non-inference traffic (pipeline runs, notebook activity) — future
  strategies will adopt the HLR-4 schema
- Long-term audit storage and retention tooling (customer-provided)

## Open Questions

None — the audit sink interface is the standard cluster logging forwarder.

# Define and publish the common inference audit event schema

## Description

Defines and publishes the common audit event schema that all inference audit events must conform to. The schema captures caller identity, model/version, timestamp, and response status — and explicitly excludes request and response payloads. It is the contract that the KServe audit emission capability builds against, and the foundation that future components (pipelines, workbenches) will adopt to emit compatible events.

## Scope

- Define a structured audit event schema covering caller identity, model and version, timestamp, and response status
- Explicitly exclude inference request and response payloads from the schema
- Ensure events formatted per the schema are deliverable to and consumable by the standard cluster logging forwarder (the cluster audit sink)
- Publish the schema so future emitting components (Data Science Pipelines, workbenches) can adopt it and emit compatible events
- Decide and document the schema's versioning/evolution approach (implementing team's decision)

## Acceptance Criteria

- The schema defines fields for caller identity, model/version, timestamp, and response status
- The schema does not include request or response payloads
- A sample event formatted per the schema is accepted by the standard cluster logging forwarder
- The schema is published in the team's agreed location and is referenceable by future emitting components
- Schema review is completed with the serving team and stakeholders

## HLR Traceability

- HLR-4 (P2): A common audit event schema is defined and published so future components (pipelines, workbenches) emit compatible events
- Supports HLR-1 (P0): the schema is the format HLR-1's events must conform to

# Emit audit events for KServe inference traffic with at-least-once delivery

## Description

Implements audit event emission in the KServe serving path: every inference request through a KServe endpoint produces a structured audit event conforming to the common audit event schema, and events are delivered to the cluster audit sink with at-least-once semantics, surviving component restart. This epic also provides the per-project enable/disable configuration surface that the serving side honors and that the Dashboard administration control writes.

## Scope

- Instrument the KServe inference request path to emit one audit event per inference request (applicability across serverless and raw deployment modes is the implementing team's decision)
- Audit event content per the common audit event schema: caller identity, model/version, timestamp, response status — no request or response payloads
- Deliver events to the standard cluster logging forwarder (cluster audit sink)
- At-least-once delivery semantics with durable buffering so events are not lost on component restart (the buffering mechanism — e.g., spooling or queueing — is the implementing team's decision)
- Per-project enable/disable configuration honored by the serving side, so inference auditing can be toggled per project
- Unit and integration tests for emission, delivery, and restart survival

## Acceptance Criteria

- Every inference request through a KServe endpoint emits an audit event containing caller identity, model/version, timestamp, and response status
- Audit events conform to the common audit event schema
- No request or response payloads appear in audit events
- Events are delivered to the cluster audit sink with at-least-once semantics
- Restarting the emitting component under traffic does not lose already-generated audit events
- Inference auditing can be enabled and disabled per project via the serving-side configuration surface; disabled projects emit no inference audit events
- The change passes the existing KServe build pipeline

## HLR Traceability

- HLR-1 (P0): Every inference request through a KServe endpoint emits an audit event capturing caller identity, model/version, timestamp, and response status (not payloads)
- HLR-2 (P0): Audit events are delivered to the cluster audit sink with at-least-once semantics and are not lost on component restart
- Supports HLR-3 (P1): provides the per-project configuration surface that the Dashboard administration control writes

# Dashboard administration control for per-project inference auditing

## Description

Adds an administrative control in the RHOAI Dashboard that enables administrators to enable and disable inference auditing per project. The control writes the per-project audit configuration surface defined and honored by the serving-side audit emission capability; the Dashboard itself owns no data plane and acts through Kubernetes CRs.

## Scope

- Project-level administration surface for toggling inference auditing per project (placement consistent with existing Dashboard settings patterns is the implementing team's decision)
- Write the per-project audit setting through the configuration surface the serving side honors (Dashboard reads and writes Kubernetes CRs)
- Restrict the control to project administrators via OpenShift OAuth project-scoped RBAC
- Reflect the current audit-enabled state accurately in the project view
- Unit and integration tests for the control and RBAC behavior

## Acceptance Criteria

- An administrator can enable and disable inference auditing for a project from the Dashboard
- The setting persists and is reflected accurately when the view is reloaded
- Non-administrator users cannot change the audit setting
- Toggling the control changes the serving side's behavior: audit events are emitted when auditing is enabled and none are emitted when disabled
- The change passes the existing Dashboard build pipeline

## HLR Traceability

- HLR-3 (P1): Administrators can enable/disable inference auditing per project from the Dashboard

decomposition_quality 5/5 — SCORE: 5

**Dimension 1 — HLR coverage: solid.** All five HLRs map to epics (HLR-1/2 → E002, HLR-3 → E003, HLR-4 → E001, HLR-5 → E004), nothing orphaned. Critically, this case's trap is handled exactly right: E001 maps only to HLR-4 (P2), but the strategy's own note says HLR-1 cannot ship before the schema is settled — E001 correctly inherits P0, and E002 (the P0 emission epic) correctly depends on it. The failure mode this case probes (schema epic left at P2 while P0 work depends on it) does not occur. E003 stays P1 correctly: the only epic depending on it is the docs epic, and docs-authoring edges don't push priority upstream. E004's P0 is derived via the docs-authoring exception, which the rubric exempts.

**Dimension 2 — epic boundaries: solid.** One component/team tuple per epic (KServe/Serving ×2, Dashboard/Dashboard, Documentation). No duplication: E001 defines the schema that E002 consumes; E002 defines the config surface that E003 writes — complementary halves of each interface, not independently built duplicates. Content authoring is isolated in E004. E002 is the largest epic (instrumentation, delivery, buffering, config surface, tests) but is one coherent serving-path change; splitting HLR-1 emission from HLR-2 durability would fragment the same request-path change. Assigning the schema epic to KServe/RHOAI Serving is defensible as first-consumer/contract-owner, and the summary flags team confirmation.

**Dimension 3 — DAG quality: solid.** All five Mermaid edges exactly match frontmatter `dependencies` (E002:[E001], E003:[E002], E004:[E001,E002,E003]), arrows run dependency → dependent, no cycles. Edges are justified: E001→E002 is a genuine build-against contract mandated by the strategy's own note; E002→E003 is a build-against on the config surface the serving side honors (consistent with the Dashboard owning no data plane); the three edges into E004 are docs-last. The E002→E003 serialization is defensible since the Dashboard writes a surface E002 defines. Critical path 4 is within the heuristic.

**Dimension 4 — scope fidelity: solid.** No invented API paths, CRD fields, env vars, or response formats. Open decisions (buffering mechanism, schema format, UI placement, deployment-mode applicability) are explicitly deferred to implementing teams rather than designed. The RBAC reference in E003 reflects the platform's existing auth model from architecture context, not invention. No epic body references sibling draft IDs — cross-epic references use capability descriptions throughout. The "tamper-evident" language absent from any HLR is correctly flagged as a strategy-author gap rather than silently scoped in or out.

**Dimension 5 — acceptance criteria: solid.** ACs are testable and traceable: per-request emission with required fields, payload exclusion, at-least-once delivery, restart survival under traffic, per-project toggle behavior end-to-end, RBAC restriction, persistence on reload. Rule-mandated ACs are present where expected: the feature-flag/disable AC on the KServe epic (satisfying the rollback/feature-flag mandate for serving-request-handling changes), build-pipeline-green on E002 and E003, and technical-review-against-implementation on the docs epic. E001's review-and-publication ACs are verifiable.

The decomposition meets every expectation the annotation sets for this case: schema epic inherits P0 with HLR-1's epic depending on it, the feature-flag AC appears on the KServe auditing epic, and docs land last. Remaining quibbles (E002's size, E003's serialization, E004's priority derivation from unverifiable frontmatter) are defensible judgment calls explicitly justified in the artifacts, not gaps. All five dimensions hold — this is a 5. | [informational] internal adversarial review score 14/14
